title: Create an account and sign in
summary: Create your account, verify your email and secure the first session.
text: Create your account Open Create account and enter your real name, email address and a unique password. One person should use one account; free promotions are protected against duplicate accounts and repeated payment identities. Submit the form: Complete the four fields and submit the registration form. The page explains any field that needs attention. Verify your email: Open the verification message and follow its link. If it does not arrive, use Resend verification from Settings and check the delivery address and spam folder. Sign in: Open Sign in. If two-factor authentication is enabled, complete the second step with your authenticator, passkey or recovery code. Secure the account Settings shows email verification, password, two-factor authentication, passkeys and active sessions. Revoke any session you do not recognise. Staff will never ask for your password, recovery codes or API keys. Enable two-factor authentication before adding payment details or production services. Next Go to Deploy your first app, or open the catalog first if you are still choosing a product.

title: Deploy your first app
summary: Choose a product, review its real requirements and follow provisioning to a working service.
text: Choose the product Open Deploy and select the product you actually want to run. Products are installed automatically from their own template; an app, a database, a game server, hosted email and a VPS do not all use the same image or setup. The product page shows its minimum resources, editable settings and current availability. A product that has not passed its deployment checks is not offered for purchase. Configure and review Choose resources: Set RAM, vCPU and storage inside the limits shown by the product. Fixed-plan products show their plan instead of resource sliders. Complete product fields: Enter only the settings shown for that product, such as a server name, token, domain or EULA acceptance. Secret values are encrypted. Review the order: Confirm the service, billing address, discount, tax, recurring total and renewal interval. Stripe handles card details; an eligible 100% discount can finish without a card charge. Follow provisioning The order and service pages show provisioning progress. Do not repeat checkout because a service is still starting. If provisioning fails, the existing order remains visible and support can retry the idempotent delivery instead of creating a duplicate. When the service is online, open Console for first-start output and use the product guide for its own setup. The generated app hostname works through HTTPS; verified custom domains can be attached later.

title: The values a product asks for
summary: When a product asks for an account, a licence or a key, and what the platform does with it.
text: Which products ask for a value Most products ask for nothing: you choose the resources and the order is enough. Some products need something that only you have, and the page of the product shows a field for each of those values before the order. A value that the product does not ask for is refused by the platform. The order is never sent with a value the product does not know. What the platform does with the values The value is sealed: The platform encrypts the value before it is written anywhere. It is kept on the instance and it is never shown again in the clear. The value goes into the container: When the instance is built, the value is written into the environment of the container, under the name the application expects. The value stays out of the address: A value is never put in the web address of the platform and never sent in a message. title: Your profile, your address and your sessions
summary: What the settings of the account hold and how to change the name, the address, the password and the sessions.
text: The profile of the account The settings of the account hold the name, the address and the password. Everything else of the account has a page of its own: the services, the domains, the invoices and the tickets. The address of the account is also where the platform writes about your services: a deployment that is finished, an invoice, a change of resources that was refused. Change the address of the account Open the settings: Choose Settings in the menu and open the panel Profile. Write the new address: Fill in the field New email address and send the form. Confirm the new address: Open the message that arrives at the new address and follow the link of the message. An address that another account already uses is refused. Only one request is open at a time: a new request replaces the one that is waiting for its confirmation. Change the password Open the settings: Choose Settings in the menu and open the panel Password. Write the new password: Fill in the three fields and save the form. The sessions of the other devices end with the change. The session you are using stays, so you are not signed out of the page you are on. The rules of the password are the same as when the account was created: at least ten characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a number. The sessions of the account The panel Sessions lists the sessions that are open for the account, with the device and the date of each one. The session you are in is marked with This device. title: Choose the right resources
summary: What the memory, the vCPU and the storage of an instance mean and how the price follows them.
text: The three resources An instance runs in a container with three limits. The container gets exactly what you buy, and the limits are the limits of the service until a change of resources is applied. The minimum and the maximum belong to the product in the catalog. A configuration under the minimum or over the maximum is refused. How the price follows the resources The price of a configuration is calculated by the platform from the resources you choose. The price is in euros and the period is the month. The price follows the resources and nothing else: the memory, the processors and the storage of the configuration. Every product of the catalog is priced with the same card of rates, so the same resources cost the same in every product. A product that would be cheaper because it asks for fewer resources could be bought by a customer who wants something else in it, and the resources they really use would be paid for by nobody. Every product of the catalog carries a minimum of resources. The page of the product shows the minimum in the panel Minimum resources, and the card of the product in the catalog shows the price of that smallest configuration. The card is the price of a month. A plan of a year is the twelve months of that card, and it is only quoted for a product that has a price of a year. The tab Resources of an instance shows what you bought: the purchased limits, the price of the month and, when a change is being prepared, the price the change would bring. title: Invoices and payment methods
summary: Understand checkout, invoices, subscriptions, renewals, discounts and payment methods.
text: Checkout Before payment, checkout shows every line, discount, tax, billing address, amount due now and recurring amount. Stripe collects card details. Blipmade stores provider identifiers and billing records, not your card number. Billing page Billing lists orders, invoices and one subscription per service. A new subscription may not have a renewal date until Stripe has confirmed its billing period; the page must show that as pending rather than inventing a date. Use the payment portal to update the card and provider billing details. The billing address saved in Settings is used for future checkout and invoices. Free and discounted orders A promotion can reduce an eligible order, including to 100%. Free campaigns can require a verified email, limit the product and term, and reject duplicate accounts or payment identities. The review page explains the applied code before you confirm. If billing and service state disagree Do not place the order again. Open the order in Billing and include its number in a support ticket. Staff can inspect the Stripe webhook, invoice, payment, fulfilment and service chain from the same order record.

title: Upgrade or resize an instance
summary: How a change of resources is ordered, what it costs and when it is applied.
text: A change of resources is an order The resources of an instance are not changed on the spot. A change is an order that has to be paid, and the service keeps the resources it has until the order is settled. The resources of a service that has not been paid for are never changed. Order the change Open the tab Resources: Open the instance and choose the tab Resources. Write the new values: Change the memory, the vCPU or the storage and choose Save resources. Pay the difference: When the change costs more, the platform writes an order for it and asks for the payment. The service is not touched before the payment. Watch the change: An increase is applied as soon as the order is paid. A decrease is settled by the platform and lowers the amount of the next invoice. When the change cannot be applied If the platform cannot apply a change that was paid for, the money goes back to you by itself: the order is marked as refunded and the instance keeps the resources it had. The event is written in the tab Activity of the instance. A change that was never paid for is simply not applied. There is nothing to refund, because the money was never taken. See Refunds and credits for the whole of the subject. Questions about a change

title: Cancel an instance
summary: What happens to an instance when you cancel it, how long it is kept and what happens to your data.
text: Cancel the instance Open the tab Settings: Open the instance and choose the tab Settings. Choose Cancel instance: The button is at the bottom of the panel. A dialog asks you to write the name of the instance to confirm. Confirm: Write the name of the instance and confirm. The instance keeps running until the end of the paid period, then it is removed. You can resume it from billing before then. What happens after the cancellation The subscription of the instance is set to end with the period that was paid. When the period is over, the instance is withdrawn and the subscription is not renewed. A cancelled instance is kept for a term of retention, thirty days by default. The data of the instance is exported before anything is deleted, and the container itself is removed only when the term is over and the operator has allowed the automatic deletion. The data of the instance is not gone when the period ends. Your data The export of the instance is written when the service is cancelled and it stays available after the service is deleted. The billing page lists the cancelled services and says whether the export is available. The export describes the service and the records of the account: the name of the instance, its product, its limits, its price, its hostnames, its events, its invoices and its payments. It is not a copy of the files of the container — a copy of the files is a backup. title: Refunds and credits
summary: When the platform returns a payment by itself, when a person decides, and what the platform does not do.
text: The refunds that are automatic There are two cases where the money goes back without anybody having to ask for it: A refund that the provider itself refuses is flagged, and the operator returns the money by hand instead of the platform keeping a payment for a service that does not exist. The refunds that are decided by a person Outside those two cases a refund is not automatic. A request is looked at by the operator and the decision is taken by a person. Open a ticket: Open the menu Support and write to the team. Describe the service, the order and what you expect. Wait for the answer: The team answers in the ticket. The platform does not promise how long a refund takes. The payment provider states the delay. Credits A decrease of the resources is not refunded. title: Attach a domain to an instance
summary: Attach a hostname, prove ownership and route it safely to an app instance.
text: Add the hostname Choose the service: Open the instance and its Domains or Network tab, then enter the full hostname you control. Publish verification DNS: Copy the TXT record exactly to your DNS provider. Verification prevents another account from claiming your hostname. Point traffic to Blipmade: Publish the target record shown by the dashboard. Keep proxying disabled while diagnosing DNS unless the page explicitly supports the proxy in front of the service. Wait for Active: Blipmade verifies DNS, creates the gateway route and provisions HTTPS. DNS and certificate issuance can take several minutes. Remove a hostname Remove it from the service before reusing it on another account. Then remove the DNS records you no longer need. Removing a hostname does not delete the service or its files.

title: The DNS records you need
summary: Which records to publish at your DNS provider, and where to read their values.
text: The records Every domain in your dashboard lists the records it expects, each with a name, a type and a value. Blipmade does not guess them and it does not write them: it tells you what to create at your DNS provider, because the DNS of your domain belongs to you. If your provider has a CNAME flattening or a proxy setting, turn it off for these records. A proxied hostname does not answer the verification check. Create the records Open the domain in the dashboard: The list of records is on the domain itself. Create them at your provider: Add one record per line, exactly as listed. Verify: Start the verification again from the domain page. Propagation Propagation is the time between creating a record and every resolver seeing it. It is usually minutes and at worst a few hours, and it depends on the TTL of your record rather than on Blipmade. A claim that is never proved runs out after seven days, so verify again as soon as your records are published. The records of a mail domain A domain of mail needs other records: the mail server that has to receive the mail, the signature of the domain and the two records that let a mail client find its settings by itself. They are listed on the domain itself in the Email page of the dashboard, and they are described in the DNS records of a mail domain. A hostname that carries both an instance and a mail domain needs both sets of records. Publish them one after the other and check each of them where it belongs.

title: The domain of the platform
summary: What apps.blipmade.com is, how it differs from a domain of yours, and which address your instance gets.
text: The domain of the platform The platform has one domain of its own: apps.blipmade.com. It is the base under which the platform reserves its names, and it is not yours to claim. The claim of the base, and of anything under it, is refused with the message That hostname is reserved by the platform. The address of an instance Open the instance: Go to the instance page and open the Network tab. Find the primary one: The panel assigns an address to every server, and the primary one is the address the service is reached at. Read it as it is: The address is an IP address and a port. It is not a name, and it carries no certificate. A hostname under the domain of the platform A hostname under apps.blipmade.com is a name of the platform. The platform keeps the name and its zone, and it reserves the whole base, so no account can claim one. Today no route of an instance is published under that base: every hostname of a customer is a hostname of a domain the customer owns. The difference is who proves the ownership and who is responsible for the DNS. For a hostname of your own, you publish the records at your provider and you prove that the hostname is yours; the platform then routes it to your instance and keeps the route up. For a name of the platform, the platform is the owner and nobody has to prove anything. A hostname of yours that is claimed for an instance is described in Attach a domain to an instance, and the records it needs are in The DNS records you need. title: Browse and edit files
summary: What the file browser of an instance can do, and what it cannot do for you.
text: Open the file browser Open the instance: Go to the files section of the instance. Walk into a folder: Open folders to see what is inside, and go back with the breadcrumb. Edit a file Open the file: Open a text file to see its content. Change it and save: Edit the content and press Save file. Saving replaces the whole file. If the application is running and holds it open, it may keep working with the old content until it is restarted. The browser also renames a file, moves or copies it into another folder of the same instance, and changes its permissions. A file that is not text is not shown in the editor: download it and change it outside. Upload and download The Folders panel of the browser has an Upload button, and every file has a Download action. The upload goes to the folder that is open in the panel. The file browser is meant for configuration and small edits. For large uploads, use the console: a download in the instance is faster and does not depend on the browser. Delete a file Select the file: Open the folder that holds the file. Delete it: Press Delete and confirm. The browser warns that the file is removed from the instance and that this cannot be undone. There is no trash folder, and nothing takes a copy of the file for you. Take a [backup](/docs?p=backups) before you delete something. What the browser does not do

title: Open the console
summary: A shell on the instance, straight from the dashboard, and what it is for.
text: Open the console Open the instance: Go to the console section of the instance. Wait for a prompt: The console attaches to the process of the instance as the user the application runs as. The browser asks the platform for the console, and the platform opens it on the server with the key of your account. The key never reaches the browser. What to use it for The console and the output The console shows the output as it arrives. The browser keeps the last lines it received and the platform keeps no history of them: a reload of the page loses the output, and a restart of the instance loses it for good. The details are in The logs of a service. What the console does not do Put anything you want to run on every start into the startup command of the instance. The console is for the one-off job.

title: The logs of a service
summary: Where the output of an application comes from, what the platform keeps of it, and what you have to keep yourself.
text: Where the output comes from The output of your application is written by the process that runs in the container. The console of the instance shows it while it is produced, and that is the only place the platform shows it to you. The platform does not collect the logs of your application. There is no log page in the dashboard, no log file is written for you and no history of the output is kept. What the platform keeps Keep your own log Write the log where you want it: Ask your application to write its own log to a file in the container, for example in the folder of the project. Read or download it: Open the file in the file browser of the instance, or download it. Put it in a backup: Ask for a backup of the instance and download it. summary: Your password, your sessions and the mail of your account.
text: Your session Signing in creates a session on the server and hands the browser an HttpOnly cookie. Scripts in the page cannot read it. Change your password Open the Password panel: The settings page of your account has a Password panel. Choose a password of ten characters or more: The password needs at least ten characters, with a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a digit. Save it: Press Change the password. Reset your password When you cannot sign in, the password is reset with a link that the platform mails to the address of the account. title: Instance access and secrets
summary: How you reach an instance, where its environment is read, and why there are no keys.
text: The ways in Everything you do to an instance goes through the account you signed in with. The credential of the platform stays on the server, in your account only. Environment variables Open the instance: Go to the startup and environment section of the instance. Set the variables: Add or change the variables the application needs and save. Wait for the next start: Saving the environment does not restart the instance. The values that are running are the ones the instance had when it started. Environment variables are readable by anyone who can open the instance and by everything that runs inside it. Keep tokens and database passwords out of your code. The startup command The startup command is what the instance runs when it starts. Put your migrations and your installs in it, so a restart comes back in a working state. Saving it does not restart the instance either. Using the API The API lives under /api of the same address you use for the dashboard. Requests are same-origin and carry your session cookie. Every request that changes something also needs the X-CSRF-Token header, whose value is the readable bm_csrf cookie. API keys Programmatic keys are {{planned}}. The API does not expose key management, so the dashboard does not offer a button to create one. Until then, scripts use the session of an account, which means they need the cookie and the CSRF token of a signed-in user. Do not put the session cookie of a real account into a script that runs unattended. Treat every cookie like a password.

title: Who can do what
summary: What your account can do in the dashboard, and how the back office of the platform is split.
text: In your own account Everything in the dashboard belongs to the account you signed in with. The instances, the hostnames, the tickets, the subscriptions and the files are checked against the owner on every request, and an instance of somebody else answers like an instance that does not exist. There is no second level of permission in the customer area. An account that can open an instance can read its files, run commands in it, change its environment, take a backup of it and remove it. What your account can do The roles of the back office The staff of the platform works in a back office that is separate from the customer area. It has two roles. Every permission comes in two: one to read and one to write. The areas are the customers, the orders, the services, the catalog, the prices, the tickets, the promotions, the infrastructure, the mail, the audit log, the staff and the settings of the platform. A staff member who does not hold a permission cannot hand it out either: nobody can grant more than they hold. The access to the container of a customer always goes through the credential of the customer, so the staff of the platform never reaches your files with its own privileges. title: Mailboxes and aliases
summary: What a mailbox of a mail domain is, what an alias does, and the space a mailbox may use.
text: Not available today Hosted mail is not on sale today, so there is no mail domain and no mailbox in your account today. Here is what you get when the sale opens. The mailboxes A mailbox is an address that receives mail and that you open in the webmail or in a mail client. It has a password, a space of its own and a status. The password of a mailbox is shown once, when the mailbox is created. It is not written down anywhere else, so a lost password means a new mailbox. The aliases An alias is an address that delivers into a mailbox instead of being a mailbox of its own. It is the way to have info@ and support@ reach the same mailbox, and the way to publish an address without opening it. An alias points at one mailbox, and the dashboard shows that mailbox in the column Goes to. When the mailbox goes, the aliases that deliver to it go with it: the mail system removes them, because an alias that the platform shows and the mail system does not have is an alias that delivers nowhere. The suspension of a mail service The mail service is suspended as a whole, not mailbox by mailbox. When the service is cancelled it goes through a period of grace, and it is suspended when the grace ends. The data of the service is kept through the grace and after the suspension, and the service can be brought back while it is not cancelled.

title: Backups of an instance
summary: Create, download and restore manual backups of an app instance safely.
text: What an instance backup contains A backup is an archive created by the service panel from the files of that app container. It is not a full account backup, a VPS snapshot or a guaranteed export of data stored in an external database. A backup kept only on the same node is not an independent disaster-recovery copy. Download important backups and keep them elsewhere. Create and download Open Backups: Open the instance and select Backups. The current limit and existing archives are shown there. Create the backup: Choose New backup, give it a useful name and wait for the background job to finish. Do not restart or reinstall the service while the archive is being created. Download important copies: Download the finished archive and verify that the file is not empty before relying on it. Restore Restore replaces the current container files with the selected archive. Stop writes to the service first, confirm you selected the correct backup and expect a restart. Files created after the backup can be lost. If creation fails Reload the list once, check the backup limit and try a short name. If it still fails, open a ticket linked to the service and include the time of the attempt; do not create repeated jobs continuously.

text: The status page Open the status page: The page is called Service status and lives at /status. It needs no session. title: Limits and fair use
summary: The bounds the platform really enforces, and the ones it does not have.
text: The limits of your instance Every product in the catalog has a minimum and a maximum for memory, CPU and disk. The configurator refuses anything outside those values, so an instance can never ask for more than the plan allows. A change of plan is checked against the same numbers. Those bounds come from the catalog itself. You do not have to remember them: the form shows what is allowed. The limits you can hit Some of these limits are not written where you would meet them. They are here, with the number the platform really uses. What is not limited Blipmade does not publish quotas for traffic, tickets, accounts or the number of instances you may run. Staying within your resources An instance that is used only as it was deployed — the application, its configuration and its data — is what the platform is built for. Backups No automatic backup is turned on for you. You choose, in the Backups tab of the instance, to run one every day or every Sunday at 03:30 UTC, or to take one by hand. The oldest unlocked backup is removed to make room for the next one, so lock the ones you want to keep. You know what the data is and how it should be restored. What the platform does offer is a manual backup of the files of the container, taken from the Backups tab of the instance. It is an archive you can download, and restoring it replaces the files of the container with the archive. It holds no dump of a database that runs somewhere else, so the copy of a database is yours to take. Take your own copy with the commands on the page of your product.
